How medfit computes estimates and uncertainty

Source: vignettes/articles/computation-algorithms.qmd

This page follows the implementation in R/effect-se.R, R/bootstrap.R, R/sem-ml.R, R/sem-optim.R, R/sem-constraints.R, R/sem-anova.R, and R/sem-mbco.R. The Methods and Formulas article defines the mediation effects; here the focus is how the computer obtains their estimates.

Delta-method standard errors

Let \(\hat\theta\) be a vector of fitted path parameters, \(V\) its estimated covariance matrix, and \(h(\theta)\) an effect such as the simple indirect effect \(h(a,b)=ab\). The gradient \(g\) lists how much the effect changes for a small change in each parameter. For \(ab\), \(g=(b,a)^\mathsf{T}\) in \((a,b)\) order. A first-order approximation gives

\[ \operatorname{SE}\{h(\hat\theta)\} \approx \sqrt{g^\mathsf{T} V g}. \]

R/effect-se.R builds named gradients for each mediation data class and matches them to named rows of @vcov; tidy() and confint() use the same builder. This includes covariance between paths, not just their separate variances. For four-way effects, an opt-in adds the sampling variance of an estimated covariate mean to INTref, NDE, and TE. A missing covariance alias is reported rather than guessed.

fit_m <- lm(mediator1 ~ treatment + covariate1, mediation_demo)
fit_y <- lm(outcome ~ treatment + mediator1 + covariate1, mediation_demo)
mediation <- extract_mediation(fit_m, model_y = fit_y,
                               treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1")
generics::tidy(mediation)

Three bootstrap algorithms

Let \(B\) be the number of replicates, \(D\) the observed data, \(T\) a statistic function, \(\hat\theta\) the fitted parameter vector, and \(V\) its covariance. All three methods return an estimate; the first two also return percentile intervals from the replicate statistics. plugin computes only \(T(\hat\theta)\).

parametric:    draw B vectors theta* from Normal(theta-hat, V)
               evaluate T(theta*) for each vector
nonparametric: draw B row-index vectors, each of length n, with replacement
               for each vector, form D*, refit inside T(D*)
cluster:       draw B vectors of J cluster IDs, each of length J
               stack whole selected clusters, assigning a fresh ID per draw
               refit inside T(D*); discard failed or flagged refits

Here \(n\) is the row count and \(J\) is the number of distinct clusters. The parametric method assumes an approximately normal parameter distribution. The row method refits and therefore can capture features the parameter-normal approximation misses. The cluster method preserves within-cluster rows and keeps repeated draws separate. The resamples and parametric vectors are drawn in the parent process before parallel::mclapply() on Unix; Windows uses a sequential fallback. A fixed seed gives the same nonparametric resamples for any ncores and sequential runs. Randomness inside statistic_fn and last-digit differences from threaded numerical libraries are outside that guarantee. Pre-drawn row indices require roughly \(4nB\) bytes. See R/bootstrap.R.

library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

boot <- bootstrap_mediation(function(d) mean(d$mediator1),
                            method = "nonparametric", data = mediation_demo,
                            n_boot = 12, seed = 7)
c(estimate = boot@estimate, lower = boot@ci_lower, upper = boot@ci_upper)

0.3843265 0.3386462 0.4693752

Native SEM: from a model to a discrepancy

The native engine translates syntax into RAM matrices. Let \(A\) contain directed paths, \(S_R\) contain model variances and covariances, \(I\) be the identity matrix, and \(F\) select observed variables. The implied covariance is

\[ \Sigma(\theta) = F(I-A)^{-1}S_R(I-A)^{-\mathsf T}F^\mathsf T, \]

where \(\theta\) is the vector of free model parameters. Let \(S\) be the observed covariance computed with divisor \(n\), and \(p\) the number of observed variables. The engine minimizes the ML discrepancy

\[ Q(\theta)=\log|\Sigma(\theta)|+ \operatorname{tr}\{S\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}\}-\log|S|-p. \]

With a mean structure, let \(\bar x\) be the observed mean, \(m\) the RAM intercepts, and \(\mu(\theta)=F(I-A)^{-1}m\). The engine adds \((\bar x-\mu)^\mathsf T\Sigma^{-1}(\bar x-\mu)\) to \(Q\). It evaluates intercepts in mean-centered coordinates for numerical stability, mapping the answer back to the model’s parameterization. An unusable implied covariance gets a finite penalty, allowing the optimizer to step back. For nested models on the same data, anova() uses \(n(Q_{\rm restricted}-Q_{\rm full})\) as its likelihood-ratio statistic; it checks nesting and marks boundary p-values in attr(result, "p_valid").

fit <- fit_sem(paste("mediator1 ~ a*treatment",
                     "outcome ~ b*mediator1 + cp*treatment", sep = "\n"),
               mediation_demo)
c(discrepancy = fit@f, n = fit@n_obs)

Constraints, acceptance, and starts

For a linear constraint \(c(\theta)=a^\mathsf T\theta+b\), the code scales \(a\) to unit length. If \(u\) contains each parameter’s natural unit, the solver works in \(x=\theta/u\) coordinates. SLSQP receives analytic objective gradients, constant Jacobians for linear rows, and recomputed numerical Jacobians for nonlinear rows. Dependent equality rows and inequalities implied by them can be removed from the solver input, but the acceptance gate checks all original rows.

A solver success code is only the first check. The gate accepts statuses 1, 3, or 4, checks every constraint’s residual in natural units (at most \(10^{-6}\)), and checks the objective on directions that preserve active constraints and bounds. Call an orthonormal basis for those directions \(Z\), the gradient in solver units \(g_x\), and the relevant Hessian of the Lagrangian \(H_L\). The reduced gradient is \(g_r=Z^\mathsf T g_x\) and reduced Hessian is \(H_r=Z^\mathsf T H_L Z\). The Newton decrement \(\sqrt{g_r^\mathsf T H_r^{-1}g_r}\) must be at most \(10^{-3}\). After dividing each Hessian row and column by the square root of its diagonal entry, the smallest eigenvalue must be at least \(10^{-4}\). This catches a stationary but nearly flat or wrong-curvature point. The gate checks active-bound multiplier signs and rejects a wrong-sign bound; the active-inequality multiplier-sign check warns without rejecting. These thresholds and verdicts are in R/sem-optim.R and R/sem-constraints.R.

An accepted nonlinear fit can receive a Newton polish: short steps solve the active-set Karush–Kuhn–Tucker equations using \(H_L\). A polished point is kept only if the objective improves and it passes the gate again; a restoration from a roundoff-limited stall is held to a cap on the objective’s rise instead (the Methods and Formulas article derives it). With nonlinear constraints, the engine tries all starts and keeps the accepted point with the smallest discrepancy. A feasible unconstrained solution can certify the optimum; otherwise the optimum diagnostic reports whether starts agreed, disagreed, or only one was accepted. A fit with only linear rows stops after the first accepted start. More starts improve the search, but agreement among starts alone is not a proof of a global optimum.

model <- paste("mediator1 ~ a*treatment",
               "outcome ~ b*mediator1 + cp*treatment", "cp == a*b", sep = "\n")
fit <- fit_sem(model, mediation_demo)
fit@diagnostics$optimum
fit@diagnostics$decrement

A zero product is a union of simpler models

For \(k\) labeled paths, \(\prod_{j=1}^k a_j=0\) means at least one path is zero. R/sem-fit.R splits explicit zero-product equalities into linear branches, fits each from a clean default start, and keeps the accepted branch with the lowest discrepancy. It supports at most 64 raw combinations of parser-produced factors, duplicates included; the limit is checked with overflow-safe arithmetic before the grid is allocated, and an over-limit model is refused on that count alone, with nothing fitted. A node that holds zero-product rows records branch_map in the ledger: structural restriction-set IDs for the raw rows (duplicate or permuted products collapse), not an affine-equivalence certificate; every raw row still runs in its original order. A branch whose equalities contradict by literal syntax (a == 0 with a == 1) is certified empty, kept in the ledger with its proof and an unavailable likelihood, and not fitted; a numerical failure is never such a proof, and an all-empty union stops with medfit_sem_empty_union. If a branch cannot be fitted, fit_sem() stops with an error rather than returning the best of the others, which need not be the constrained optimum; the error carries the outcome ledger of every required branch as $ledger, and a fit’s ledger is fit@diagnostics$ledger. If the optimizer accepts a fit and only the covariance stage fails, fit_sem() stops with medfit_sem_covariance_error, which carries the accepted likelihood in its ledger and is never a fit; inside mbco_sem() such a null keeps its likelihood and a warning. A complete enumeration is not a certificate of a global optimum. This avoids a zero Jacobian where several factors vanish. mbco_sem() uses the same logic for an indirect-effect test: fit each single-path null, use the smallest likelihood-ratio statistic, and refer it to a one-degree-of-freedom chi-square distribution when its regularity conditions hold. A null on a boundary can invalidate that reference, so inspect its warning.

base <- paste("mediator1 ~ a*treatment",
              "outcome ~ b*mediator1 + cp*treatment", sep = "\n")
full <- fit_sem(base, mediation_demo)
mbco_sem(full, paths = c("a", "b"))
null <- fit_sem(paste(base, "a*b == 0", sep = "\n"), mediation_demo)
null@internals$branch
